title: Leap Life
summary: Saul Williams discusses Leap Life, collaboration with Carlos Niño, political histories and using the human voice as a primary instrument. He reflects on the ideas and collaborative work behind his first solo album in more than a decade.
transcript:
And RRR, Lauren here with you on Breaking and Entering.

We're about to jump in very soon to a chat with the one and only Saul Williams, but I did play a bracket of Saul Williams-related tracks.

They're all friends and collaborators on his brand-new record, his first solo album in over a decade, Leap Life, that came out last week.

We heard at the top there from the wonderful Jimetta Rose and the Voices of Creation, who Voices of Creation are sort of a community-based choir that are led by vocalist and songwriter Jimetta Rose, who's sort of a mainstay of the Los Angeles scene.

Quite to reset that one called Let the Sunshine In and followed it up with Gonjasufi, who I haven't heard from in a little while, but really great to see that Gonjasufi is collaborating with Saul Williams on this brand-new record, and what a chance to revisit his incredible debut record from back in 2010.

I'm pretty sure that would have been an album of the week at RRR back in the day, A Sufi and a Killer from Gonjasufi, who is Sumac X.

It was put out on Warp Records and produced by Flying Lotus, The Gaslamp Killer and Mainframe.

We heard Sheep from Gonjasufi, and also out of LA as well from Georgia Anne Muldrow, incredible producer and co-founder of SomeOthaShip Connect with Dudley Perkins.

Great Blacks was the name of the track, lifted from a record from back in 2015 called A Thoughtiverse Unmarred.

And we just heard from Saul Williams there revisiting a track from his second solo album, an iconic track from his self-titled release from 2004, list of demands.

And, yeah, it was a real honour to chat recently with the legendary Saul Williams, who was only in the country quite recently back in June here in Melbourne, doing a few shows as part of Rising Festival, some shows with his longtime collaborator Carlos Niño and friends.

He was part of Day Tripper and appeared as part of the Vinyl Factory Reverb sessions that are happening at ACMI for a sort of deep listening and talk session there.

It's really hard to, yeah, put a label on Saul Williams.

He's a true renaissance man, a multidisciplinary artist, just balancing so many different creative roles from music to writing and poetry as a filmmaker as well.

And, of course, as an actor most recently in his critically acclaimed role as the preacher Jedidiah Moore in the film Sinners.

For nearly three decades now, Saul Williams has operated at the intersection of language and rhythm.

He's a true icon of spoken word, really helped put, I guess, slam poetry on the map and has been shattering the boundaries of poetry and punk and hip-hop and political resistance throughout his incredible career.

His voice has been a real force for political activism and systematic critique.

And his new project, Leap Life, sees him pushing that even further.

He's operating sort of on the core philosophy that the voice is the instrument.

And he expands on what the definition of music itself can be and what it means to trust the moment.

It sees him working again with Carlos Niño on this new record.

And as mentioned, a bunch of incredible guests, a really stacked line-up on this album, including Gonjasufi, who you heard from, Georgia Anne Muldrow, Jimetta Rose, Kamasi Washington, who I played for you earlier, Robert Del Naja, 3D from Massive Attack, Moor Mother and many, many others.

The title of the album itself, Leap Life, comes from Saul's own leap year birthday.

He was born on the 29th of February.

So technically, he's only 13 years old, having 13 official birthdays in his lifetime.

So it also feels incredibly intentional that his new album features 13 songs, which each hold a completely different worldview.

Saul Williams has described Leap Life as not a conventional studio album, but as a gathering of spirits, histories, frequencies and unfinished revolutions.

And so I began my chat with Saul Williams, chatting about gathering spirits and histories and how he captured that energy and asked him if the recording process felt more like an archive or a seance.

I mean, it definitely had a certain type of seance energy, only in that things were aligned so smoothly.

It felt as if there were forces at work in that, in putting together this album, I hadn't beforehand really thought very thoroughly about putting together an album.

The album really came together through Carlos's enthusiasm and insistence that it was time.

And I went into the studio kind of like fresh with a bunch of music that I'd made, but with no lyrics attached, and just went in there and knocked it out.

You mentioned Carlos just then, who you toured with here in Melbourne.

You've had a really long working relationship with Carlos Niño as your percussionist, producer, and I guess he's been named as a musical architect, sort of sequencing your new record too.

Can you tell me about your relationship with Carlos?

Because it seems like a very important one in your life.

Yeah.

I mean, actually, the first time I ever was flown to LA to perform, it was by Carlos.

And that was when the first single or EP that I ever came out with on Big Dada came out, which was like over 20 years ago.

That's how we met.

It's at that night with the show with Carlos that I ended up meeting my first producer, Rick Rubin, and a bunch of things that, you know, turned into this career happened after that first meeting.

So we worked together in like promotional capacity before, like you would put on shows, what have you, but we hadn't worked together.

And that was a creative capacity, but we hadn't worked together in a music studio.

And we decided that we were going to work together a little over a year ago and decided that we would announce that we would go into the studio to work on Leap Life.

And that, in order to announce that, we put together a concert.

That concert became our last album, the Tree People album, which was not intended as an album.

It was just a show to announce that we were going into the studio to work on this album, Leap Life.

The new record, Leap Life, perhaps beginning with the title itself, it points directly to your own leap year birthday.

I guess because your birthday is actually, you know, so rare, it happens once every four years.

Do you feel like you've got a certain unique relationship with time in that way?

A hundred percent.

You know, when you have a birthday like that, you begin by asking like, well, why don't I have a birthday this year?

Who created the calendar?

Who created the, you know, whose practice of time are we practicing?

What do you mean the Gregorian calendar?

Who's Gregory?

Who's Pope Gregory?

Why would the church determine that?

You know, all of this stuff.

So, of course, it began a long process of questioning.

And those questions do have answers.

And when you learn the distinctions between our calendar and, let's say, many indigenous calendars, you know, where there are 13 moons in a cycle and 28 days, calendars that are, that perhaps feel way more connected to nature as we know it.

That is the root of what we call biodynamics and what have you.

You realize that the calendar, sometimes it feels like an act of disassociation, that it separates us from a true understanding of nature and aligns us with more of an alignment with the empire.

You know, so it's August and you have a Pope Augustus.

And what does that have to do with anything other than those who once ruled?

In preparation for this interview, yeah, I realized I'd never really, yeah, sort of considered why, you know, leap years actually exist.

But, yeah, obviously they exist to keep our clocks aligned as well with the Earth's orbit.

Do you see, like, leap life itself, your record as, like, I don't know, a tool for realigning, like, the human perspective, perhaps?

I like that idea.

Conceptual.

But, yeah, that is the goal.

I mean, the realigning that has to occur now, obviously, there is, there are forces at work to maintain a sort of sociopolitical alignment with, you know, colonialism and acts of the past.

You have a lot of people in power who are focused on keeping things a particular way.

And, yes, the power of music, which has always been born of ceremony, that has always been used to mobilize, does have that power to realign and to remind us of our power as people, as listeners, to harmonize, to be a threat to power.

And so, yeah, that energy is certainly in leap life.

And this new record sees you so expanding on what the definition of music itself can be.

It mentions operating on the philosophy that the voice is the instrument.

This new record, the vocal focus, also feels, as you were saying, like, deeply ceremonial and has this real sort of spiritual invocation.

How do you view the relationship between the voice as, like, a tool for political agitation versus, like, a vessel for a more spiritual realm?

I mean, those two are connected.

Those are not, like, separate ideas.

It's the same idea.

It's really just the realization of what one's voice is connected to.

And with that realization comes an understanding, perhaps, of, I mean, responsibility sounds like a heavy word, but I do think that those in power, like, in the U.S., where I'm from, for example, who throw around words like freedom, I think they use those words like freedom to avoid talking about their responsibilities, you know.

And so I think that a voice, you know, obviously can do a lot.

You know, when we sing, there's so much power and beauty in singing.

The voice reflects, you know, the possibilities of humanity.

And not only through the sounds we make, but through the meaning that we're able to emit.

And some voices are used manipulatively.

And I think there's also a role for the voice to play in working to not be manipulative, but working to open up something or to remind someone of something.

And I think that there are spiritual and political aspects to that that are intertwined.

And you said recently that we need our discontent to be voiced.

We need that type of energy on our airwaves right now.

What do you think, yeah, I guess happens to society when it's like collective discontent is, you know, systematically quietened or filtered out?

Well, when it's quietened or filtered out, I think that we begin to make a series of whether it's mistakes or what have you, but essentially art, music, entertainment becomes just that entertainment.

I mean, it becomes something that's there to escape, to distract.

It ceases to be a threat to power.

It serves as an arm of state propaganda, of capitalism.

None of these things are crucial to art.

Art, you know, theater, music have disrupted society in the past, have reminded people of what they're capable of.

You think of a play like Shakespeare's Julius Caesar and the role of Mark Antony's speech there, you know, which he has to give after promising those in power who've just murdered, you know, their leader, that he won't say anything against them.

And so he has to find a very careful way of getting the people to be reminded that they have the power to overturn the stakes and what have you.

There's a certain tendency that we have.

I mean, it's not like we want to fight or we want to mobilize, we want to have to overthrow, but there are times when you must, when we can't allow things to continue the way they are, right?

And so, and at that moment, it becomes all of our responsibility to do everything within our power, within our reach to shift things, right?

So if you're a DJ, you have stuff to play, if you're a musician, you have music to make, if you're a teacher, you have stuff that you need to instill in students.

If you, you know, if you're, you know, there's, it doesn't matter what your lane is, there's a way in which it plays out.

[Unclear audio at 00:12:53–00:16:29]

And Travella from the new Saul Williams record, Leap Life, the track Conspiracy, on Breaking and Entering.

And if you've just joined us, we are in the middle of a recent interview that I did.

It was a real honour to catch up with the legendary Saul Williams, as mentioned earlier.

Yeah, just a true multidisciplinary artist balancing so many different creative roles, from acting and directing and writing and poetry.

Yet he said that making music is an act of daily necessity for him and has described the process as a way of both zoning out and zoning in.

So we begin the second part of my chat with Saul Williams as he takes us inside his daily practice.

I asked him, how does the act of making music allow him to detach from the noise of the world while simultaneously sharpening his focus?

Well, typically, you know, whether I'm reading or writing or just, you know, living my life in whatever capacity, I'm listening to music, it's there.

Music is there.

And at certain moments, there are times when you're kind of searching for something, whether it's sonically or energetically.

A lot of times I turn to music in those moments, whether it's music I've made, you know, or not.

Most times it's music I've not made, music that I'm listening to of others.

But there are times when even that music doesn't touch the thing I'm trying to touch.

And that's when I end up, you know, diving into creating sounds or exploring sounds in order to achieve just an idea.

It may be four or five minutes, it may be for five hours.

But, you know, the ideas begin to accumulate.

And yes, it is a part of a kind of creative ecosystems because it's one thing to be searching for words.

It's another thing to be searching for sounds.

Beyond or within a so-called kind of silence, silence in that I'm not using words.

So I'm speaking about the process of music instrumentally, initially for me.

Like for me, usually when I'm writing a song, I start with music and eventually words will come.

As I was describing earlier with the recording of this album, a lot of the music I started composing, but not with an album in mind.

It's just kind of filling a space.

And yeah, it does feed something, but not to the point where it delicited like me putting words to it.

Some of that music that's on that album, I sat with literally for years without words.

And not until that brief moment in the studio with Carlos that I decided I was ready to put words on those songs.

So you have so many incredible collaborators on this new album, Leap Life as well.

Kamasi Washington, Georgia Anne Muldrow, Gonjasufi, Moor Mother and Robert Del Naja, of course, 3D from Massive Attack, who, yeah, they were in Australia recently doing some really incredible shows here.

But I understand, yeah, Robert gifted you with some soundscapes on this new record.

Can you tell that story?

Robert and I have been exchanging music, musical ideas for years.

We've been exchanging files.

We even have an album, Robert, me, and Gonjasufi, that's never been released.

Amazing.

Can you put that out, please?

I want to.

I can't wait until we get.

Yeah.

And so that process began with Robert, like, it started over a decade ago.

And so since then, whenever we have something we want to share, we just share it.

So sometimes some mornings I wake up with a surprise email like, yo, I was thinking of you.

Check this out.

And so that happened not so recently at one point where it was a bunch of sounds that he had been playing with.

And he was like, you know, feel free to play with these if it comes up.

And so there are three songs on Leap Life that are from stuff that Robert sent me that I either began to play with and chop up and add sounds to, or that I used exactly as he sent.

Those songs are Controlled is Not Controllable.

I Think I Get It Now and Not Everything For Sale.

And so Robert played a part.

Gonjasufi played a part.

Like you said, Moor Mother, Kamasi Washington, Jimetta Rose.

These are all friends.

Like, it's really like if I were to piece together an army of people that I trust and have worked with, this is them.

I did want to ask as well, there's a new book that you've announced is coming out very soon, too, called Songs My Mother Taught Me, Why the Artist Must Take Sides, which is about your relationship to politics.

Is that correct?

It's about my relation to politics and I guess in a more general sense, how I've grown to relate art to politics.

It's kind of my response to the question, what radicalized you?

You know, basically, last year, 2025, around, probably around the month of February, after, you know, already two years of witnessing all of the horrors that all of us across the world have been witnessing happening in the world and led by Western government.

I decided that it was time to shift gears and aside from the importance of, you know, doing what we can from our positions to like boost Palestinian voices and, you know, trying to recapture the algorithm, you know, so to speak, try to make sure that things aren't covered up or what have you.

I felt that it was time to like shift gears towards stuff, towards the practices that I know best and trust, which, of course, are music, poetry, and performance.

And so between March and August of last year, I recorded Leap Life and I wrote Songs My Mother Taught Me.

And so those two projects and Songs My Mother Taught Me, of course, we've discussed Leap Life, and that's one aspect of a kind of process for me.

And then Writing Songs My Mother Taught Me, I didn't really know how this book would come out.

I just knew that I had to get these ideas out just because it seemed as if a lot of, I mean, I was being asked repeatedly, what do you think is the role of an artist during this time?

And I'm no philosopher or what have you, but I can tell the story of how I came to see my role as an artist.

And that's what Songs My Mother Taught Me is about.

I guess my final question for you, Saul, you've stated that you don't really fuck with hope, and you've cited the Audre Lorde poem where she writes that hope is counter-revolutionary, pressure cooks.

I guess in that way, do you see hope as being more of like a passive thing?

And yeah, if so, what sort of active force replaces it for you when you're creating?

I mean, to clarify, I do think that hope serves a purpose.

And it's nice to have a sense of hope and to be able to trust that the process, that your work, that your vision is not in vain, or our vision of humanity and what we're working for, the kind of world we want to see, that this work is not in vain and that we have the potential to transform society and transform ourselves.

However, I also see, you know, I have an album that came out in 2008 called The Inevitable Rise and Liberation of Niggy Tardust.

And the word inevitable was always the key word for me, although the public always fixated on Niggy Tardust.

But it's the inevitable that was crucial in my understanding, was that, you know, for example, some would say that socialism is the science of life.

That the only way that we can progress as humanity is through reminding ourselves of our relationship to nature, of the responsibilities that we have to each other, and making sure that our, you know, societies represent us, all of us, properly.

That, you know, that we don't extract so much from the earth, that we extract ourselves, that we find the balance.

And I believe that that is a balance that we have to achieve together.

And so I've never really understood the process of what we're fighting for as something that we have to put our hope towards.

Yes, there is, yes, there are active ingredients, right?

And it's the active ingredients of hope, the ones that contain work, the ones that contain study, the ones that contain organizing, the ones that contain focus.

Yes, it also, you know, embodies play and dance and all of these things.

I mean, we look at the dance floor as a battlefield or as a training ground, like these are all necessary aspects of what it means to be alive, as is love and making love and all of these things.

They all play crucial parts in our evolution, in understanding what love is in its broadest sense.

But I've just felt like there's a way in which some people lean on hope that is maybe unhealthy.

And I've never really thought that the process of Indigenous, Black and Indigenous liberation being something that is rooted in hope.

It's rooted in an inevitability, because if we don't shift our relationship to each other, to the land, what have you, we'll be forced to live under the rule of all of the dudes that none of us can stand.

The Peter Thiel, you know, I'm blanking on the other guy's name, the Tesla guy, which is funny.

I never blank on his name, but I'm happy to.

Elon Musk.

Yes, you know, and the leadership and all the hypocrisy that we see.

We all see it.

We all clearly see all of the evil hypocrisy that we live under, right?

And yes, there is an inevitability that comes with the fact that we are not going to be able to sustain a relationship to power as long as power is in hand such as those.

And so there is an inevitability in it, and it has nothing to do with hope.

It has more to do with their projection or belief in our hopelessness that we will be forced to be surveyed, controlled, and there's nothing we can do about it.

Well, thank you so much, Saul.

Thank you so much for being so generous with your time today, and congratulations on Leap Life.

It's an incredible record, too.

Thank you.

I'm very much looking forward to, yeah, that Gonjasufi 3D Saul Williams record coming out soon.

Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

I can't wait for people to hear it.
